title: An effort to circumvent the Electoral College may be within reach. But hurdles remain
description: Voting booths are seen at Glass Elementa
body:
Voting booths are seen at Glass Elementary School's polling station in Eagle Pass, Texas, on Nov. 8, 2022.
                
                    Mark Felix/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Mark Felix/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   A national effort to ensure that only winners of the popular vote become president could reach a critical milestone soon.   It's a possible outcome of huge Democratic wins in this month's midterm elections.   Next year, Democrats will fully control five states that could sign the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, an agreement among states to award their presidential electoral votes to the winner of the nationwide popular vote, not the winner of their respective states.    
   If they do join other 18 Democratic-led states — plus the District of Columbia — that are in the compact, the effort will have surpassed the needed 270 electoral votes required to go into effect, making an end run around the Electoral College. So far no Republican-led states have joined the compact and the party is largely not unified on the issue.   There are still plenty of political, practical and legal hurdles that this effort would need to clear. But proponents are optimistic many of those hurdles will be cleared – even perhaps in time for the next presidential election.   "I've never been more confident that 63% of American voters can get what they want in the 2028 presidential election, which is a national popular vote for president." Patrick Rosenstiel, a senior consultant to National Popular Vote, the group pushing for the compact in states across the country, told NPR, referencing Pew polling.   Right now, the compact has a total of 222 electoral votes. The five states that will soon be completely in the hands of Democrats – Arizona, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Nevada and Wisconsin – add up to 61 electoral votes. Combinations of at least four of those states would put the compact over 270.   So far, governors and incoming governors in Pennsylvania and Nevada have said they are open to signing legislation that would bring their states into the interstate agreement. But other governors have yet to publicly weigh in.   
   One of the looming questions over these efforts is whether these states – all presidential battlegrounds – would be willing to give up their immense influence in elections ahead of the 2028 presidential contests.   And leaders in each state will also have to weigh whether they want to be the tipping point in moving forward a movement that could upend how the U.S. decides presidential winners.   Already, some Democrats are more reticent on the issue than they were before. For example, Democratic Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs, who had previously supported the measure, has not commented recently on whether the state's new Democratic majorities should sign on. NPR reached out to Hobbs' office for comment but did not receive a response before publication.   And then of course, there are the various legal and logistical hurdles.    The practical and legal hurdles   Some legal scholars have observed that this agreement between states could run afoul of the compact clause in the Constitution, which says that "no state shall, without the consent of Congress … enter into any agreement or compact with another state … unless actually invaded, or in such imminent danger as will not admit of delay."   Norman Miller, a constitutional law professor at Willamette University, said that beyond the legal hurdles, he sees a range of practical issues with the compact.   Mostly, he said, it could upend what is a core feature of American presidential elections, which is that they are largely decentralized.   States individually decide who can vote and how they can vote. He said forcing electors from one state to vote according to the tallies in another state could create some tension.   "We would want to have a standardized, uniform set of rules regarding who gets to vote for president, how they vote, how those votes are tabulated, and to have a federal election authority doing that tabulation," he said. "I think trying to nationalize [the current system] and entrusting a national election to 51 separate election administrators would just sow discord and distrust."   
   But John Koza, the chairman of National Popular Vote, said if the compact works the way it is supposed to, none of that will be necessary.   
   "We don't need a centralized bureaucracy or a presidentially appointed commission that could be manipulated," he told NPR. "The simple fact is current state and federal law provide for the issuance of a certified vote count from each state. And all that has to be done is add them up."   But mostly, Miller said the biggest question before this effort is whether such a large reform should be done via a constitutional amendment.   Upending the Electoral College, some argue, would be a profound change to how the U.S. chooses the leader of the free world. Opponents of a national popular vote, such as Save Our States, argue that without the incentives created by the Electoral College, American politics will move more toward "toward more regional politics and would exacerbate existing divides."   Miller said even though it will be much more difficult to pull off, it would be worth going through a more fulsome process via Article 5 to get rid of the Electoral College, instead of working around it.   "This is where I think process matters," he said. "If you really want to have a national popular vote for the president and avoid all of the legal and practical difficulties, you need to do that through a constitutional amendment, because only a constitutional amendment can address the legal and practical challenges of conducting a national popular vote for the presidency."   A similar effort to pass an amendment to get rid of the Electoral College in 1969 failed, though. And very few amendments have even gotten close to passing in recent history.   Rosenstiel, the consultant to the National Popular Vote, said this is why he thinks groups like his are seeking a creative solution to something most Americans agree is a problem.   
   And, he said, he ultimately thinks a national popular vote will solve multiple problems at once. For one, he said, it will force presidential candidates to appeal to most of the country, as opposed to a select group of voters in battleground states.   And, importantly, he said, it would make all voters feel like their vote matters.   "We should have a system where every American citizen feels valued and is valued when they cast their vote," he said. "And there's only one reform that delivers it."

title: How a GOP redistricting 'dummymander' in North Carolina backfired by 2 seats

      In North Carolina, Republican lawmakers redrew voting maps, aiming to  gain one seat in Congress. Instead, they lost two seats, in a classic example of what political scientists call a "dummymander."

title: The latest from Trump's press conference
description: President Trump gave a wide-ranging press conference following his historic trip to Asia where he met with Chinese President Xi and Russian Pre
body:
President Trump gave a wide-ranging press conference following his historic trip to Asia where he met with Chinese President Xi and Russian President Putin.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    AILSA CHANG, HOST:  President Trump returned to Washington after his three-day trip to Asia and took questions from the White House today. The trip included the first ever three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. But there was little in the way of agreements on key global issues.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: The United States entered this trip from a position of unmatched economic and diplomatic strength.CHANG: Well, all of this raises questions about the staying power of Trump's America-first approach and America's future role in the world. Joining us now is NPR White House correspondent Franco Ordoñez, who is in the room, and we have NPR national security correspondent Greg Myre. Hello to both of you.FRANCO ORDOÑEZ, BYLINE: Hello.GREG MYRE, BYLINE: Hi, Ailsa.CHANG: All right. So, Franco, did the president make any news in this press conference?ORDOÑEZ: Yeah, I mean, not really. I mean, it was really a very meandering talk, starting off with highlights of his first two years in office. And then he probably spent about 30 minutes talking about his time abroad and, you know, recounting his relationship with Xi and Putin. He did say, though, that he and Xi had made some agreements about putting in guardrails - that's the word he used - with artificial intelligence, which he calls super intelligence. Here he is there.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)TRUMP: It's not artificial intelligence. It's not artificial. It's super. Problem is, it may be too super. So President Xi and I agree that we're going to do some joint guardrails, the two of us, 'cause there really is no third place.ORDOÑEZ: Now, of course, details are scarce, but the idea of guardrails is notable because Trump has pretty - previously, at least, been pretty allergic to any restrictions on developing AI. I mean, he has repeatedly said he's wanted to maintain a U.S. advantage over China.CHANG: Right. OK, well, Greg, Trump had some things to say about chip sales to China and the whole Nvidia fallout, right? What struck you about his answers there?MYRE: Yeah, I mean, Trump says he wants the U.S. to keep the lead in AI, as Franco just noted. And he also said he won't allow U.S. companies to build AI data centers outside the U.S. However, Trump is the one allowing Nvidia to sell advanced chips to China. Nvidia's Jensen Huang lobbied Trump last year and persuaded the president to allow these sales. And just yesterday, the House Foreign Affairs Committee released a list of requests this year by Nvidia and another chipmaker, AMD, to sell chips to Chinese company - companies. As of May this year, the Trump administration approved the sale of nearly 900,000 advanced chips, and they include big names like Alibaba and Tencent. And those two companies are also on a Pentagon list of Chinese firms that are linked to the Chinese military. So what does Trump actually want here? Does he want Nvidia to keep selling those chips to China, or does he want to block those sales?CHANG: Good questions. Well, Trump was also asked about the whole change in leadership over cybersecurity, right? What did we learn there?MYRE: Yeah, Trump fired the White House Cybersecurity Director Sean Carncross, and at the press conference today, he said, I don't think that person was good enough. Now, he's being replaced by Kirsten Davies, who's been the chief information officer at the Defense Department. And this is certainly an important position, but it's a policy position, not a hands on operational position.The agency that's really important here is CISA, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which deals with election security and protecting government networks from cyberattacks. And this agency has not had a director since Trump became president almost two years ago. Now, as it happens, Trump's nomination to lead the agency, Michael LoSapio, had a Senate confirmation hearing yesterday. He was grilled by Democratic senators. He was asked who won the 2020 presidential election. He refused to answer. He was asked if the Capitol was attacked on January 6, 2021, and he said he didn't think it was an attack. So it's not clear that he'll be confirmed, but whoever winds up in this position will be in charge of election security in 2028.CHANG: Interesting. OK, Franco, back to this meeting with Xi and Putin, which was designed to demonstrate American power, right? Do you think it also may have opened the door for allies to turn away from the U.S.?ORDOÑEZ: Yeah, I mean, very much designed to demonstrate American power, but I also think it does show that power and influence are not the same thing. I mean, Trump was asked today if Putin, who he called his friend, was also America's friend.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)TRUMP: I can't speak to America.ORDOÑEZ: You know, he really couldn't answer that. But he did continue to make the case that his relationship with Putin would reap benefits for America, though we haven't really seen that yet. You know, the war in Ukraine continues to rage on. But we are seeing allies start to build alliances with other nations as, you know, confidence in the U.S. falters, and they look to reduce their dependence on the U.S.CHANG: Well, great. What about progress when it comes to Iran? Did anything come out of this trip on that front?MYRE: The short answer is no. There's no indication the war, now nearly nine months old, was discussed in any great detail on the trip. Trump did mention it briefly at the news conference. He said what he said many times before - Iran can't have a nuclear weapon and that Iran does want to make a deal. The one significant development in recent days has been increased Iranian attacks on oil tankers and Gulf countries.CHANG: OK, Franco, real quick on domestic politics. Now, Trump was up there with Vice President Vance - right? - and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Anything strike you about what either of those men said?ORDOÑEZ: Well, I mean, both men offered really glowing support for the president. And Vance, who obviously remained in Washington for the trip, said he missed the president and even joked that he felt like he was in the movie "Home Alone."CHANG: (Laughter).ORDOÑEZ: Whereas Rubio was able to talk more authoritatively about his work and just came across as a more consequential figure. The issue for both, though, is that their association with Trump, who is, frankly, very unpopular now.CHANG: That is NPR's Franco Ordoñez and NPR's Greg Myre. Thank you to both of you.ORDOÑEZ: (Inaudible).MYRE: Sure thing, Ailsa.

title: Texas execution took over an hour as staff struggled to find vein; Reinaldo Dennes moaned about pain
description: This photo combination shows Reinaldo De
body:
This photo combination shows Reinaldo Dennes, left, on April 14, 2026 and Thomas Mitchell Overton.
                
                    Texas Department of Criminal Justice/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Texas Department of Criminal Justice/AP
    

   
   HUNTSVILLE, Texas — Texas executed Reinaldo Dennes on Thursday in a procedure that took over an hour, as prison staffers struggled to find a suitable vein for the two intravenous needles carrying the lethal dose of the sedative pentobarbital.   And once it began, he moaned repeatedly about pain, groaned several times and asked God to take him away from the pain. A prison spokesperson said all procedures were followed appropriately and suggested that Dennes might have exaggerated or faked the pain.   The execution followed renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the U.S. in the aftermath of Tennessee's failed execution in September of Christa Pike, who survived two doses of pentobarbital that her lawyers say probably did not enter her bloodstream correctly and instead pooled in her arms, leaving them burned and blistered.   
   Dennes, who was found guilty of capital murder in the death of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer found shot multiple times in his Houston office in January 1996, was the second person put to death in the country on the day, after Florida carried out a record-breaking 20th execution of the year, of Thomas Mitchell Overton.   Dennes gave a brief statement in which he said he wanted his loved ones to know he was blessed the past 30 years "knowing the love of the father." Then he told the warden: "Go, warden!"   Almost immediately he exclaimed: "The pain! Go! Go!" He uttered an expletive and implored "the father" to "take this pain." "Let me go, father," he said again and again. "Let me go. … I'm here. I've been your son all these years."   Then he shouted: "My right leg is killing me!" and described it as a cramp. After another profanity, he grunted, then said, "I don't think this is normal. Take me, father. Don't let me suffer like this. C'mon."   After three loud groans, Dennes began snoring sounds — eight of them — that progressively got quieter before a final loud snore. Then he began breathing quietly, about a dozen breaths, also getting progressively less pronounced.   
   The procedure was completed at 7:07 p.m., 63 minutes after he was strapped to the gurney. A minute later, after being examined by a physician, Dennes was pronounced dead at 7:08 p.m. at the penitentiary in Huntsville.   Prison officials said all procedures were followed appropriately. Spokesperson Amanda Hernandez acknowledged a number of unsuccessful attempts to find a suitable vein before the execution team managed to insert the needles in Dennes' left foot and on the left side of his neck.   She did not know how many attempts were unsuccessful but said the sites ultimately used were in accordance with the state's procedures.   Hernandez also suggested that Dennes may have been exaggerating the pain, saying he began complaining before the drugs began to flow and also of pain in places where there was no IV.   Asked if he was faking, she replied, "I think, yeah, there were allegations. ... There was nothing abnormal on our part."   "This isn't the first time we had to insert IVs into other locations. It's also not the first time we've had an inmate make allegations of pain immediately," Hernandez said.   Witness Janice Copeland's husband, David, was a security guard shot during the robbery. He survived his wounds and died five years ago.   "David always felt Reinaldo would outlive him. Unfortunately he was right," she said Thursday. "Finally after 30 years, justice has been served."   Earlier in the day Florida carried out its execution of Overton, 71, who was convicted of murdering a pregnant woman and her husband, Susan and Michael MacIvor, during a home invasion.   Overton was pronounced dead at 6:19 p.m. following a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison. In a final statement, he denied ever breaking into the couple's home and attacking them, saying, "I never killed anyone."   Florida has now carried out more than half the nation's 39 executions to date this year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, who has made aggressive use of the death penalty like few other governors.   
   DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said he wanted justice for families who wait decades for death sentences to be carried out. He signed the death warrants that led to a record of 19 executions in 2025, then the most in a single year in Florida since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. Florida still plans two more executions, in December.   Texas set a record for executions there when 40 people were put to death in 2000.   The executions of two men in their 70s cast a renewed spotlight on the aging of the U.S. death row population.

title: A second judge blocks Trump's arch, saying it's unlikely to succeed in court
description: President Trump holds up a model of his
body:
President Trump holds up a model of his proposed triumphal arch at a White House event in Oct. 2025. Two different federal judges have ruled against it this week.
                
                    John McDonnell/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        John McDonnell/AP
    

   
   A federal judge in Virginia plans to issue a preliminary injunction blocking President Trump's triumphal arch indefinitely.   District Judge Leonie Brinkema said during a Friday hearing that she would grant the request of the county board of Arlington, Va., which sued over the arch in October. Democracy Forward, the nonprofit representing the plaintiffs, confirmed the ruling in a statement shared with NPR.   
   "We are pleased that the court has recognized the irreparable harm that will come to people who live and work in Arlington and stopped the massive vanity project while our case is heard and considered by the court," said senior counsel Kate Talmor.   Justice Department spokesperson Matthew Nies told NPR it will appeal the decision immediately.   The 250-foot arch would be built in Memorial Circle, which is part of D.C. but sits on the Virginia side of the Potomac River, a short distance from both Arlington National Cemetery and Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, both in Arlington.   
   Arlington County has argued that the arch would "cause significant harm" to its residents in multiple ways, including increasing noise and air pollution and "clogging thoroughfares needed for emergency transport services." And it said an arch that doubles as a military complex — as Trump has suggested — would pose public safety risks and require additional county resources to manage.   Arlington also argues the arch would disrupt historic sightlines between Arlington National Cemetery and D.C.'s National Mall, and pose logistical challenges for the roughly 24 to 27 funerals the cemetery holds every weekday. The county also has concerns about air and road traffic, saying construction-related delays could cause more accidents and disrupt emergency vehicles far beyond the traffic circle.   "In the last 60 days, Arlington police, fire, and emergency units have responded to approximately 200 incidents in the area surrounding the Circle, including traffic stops and assisting with unconscious persons within Arlington National Cemetery," they wrote. "And the visitors the Arch is intended to attract will increase demand for those same emergency services."   
   The plaintiffs, like many critics of the arch, accused the Trump administration of rushing through federally mandated environmental reviews and failing to consider alternatives. The National Park Service has defended the federal review process — which ended in approval earlier this month — and said building the arch somewhere else would defeat its purpose.   "The County brings this lawsuit to halt the agency's feverish pace toward construction of the Arch and to ensure that the 'hard look' mandated by [the National Environmental Preservation Act] is completed before the agency commences disruptive and harmful ground-disturbing activities," the plaintiffs wrote last month.   
   NPR has reached out to the White House for comment. Spokesperson Davis Ingle told NPR earlier this week that the administration will "continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds."   Brinkema, an appointee of President Clinton, is the second judge to rule against the arch this week.   On Wednesday, D.C. District Judge Tanya Chutkan extended a restraining order that prevents the Trump administration from breaking ground through Dec. 3 while she considers the underlying legal arguments.   
   That case was brought earlier this year by a group that includes Vietnam War veterans and was joined by the governments of D.C. and Virginia last month. Nine Kennedy family members moved to get involved last week.   Friday's ruling goes even further, preventing construction while Arlington's legal challenge plays out.   And Brinkema suggested that Arlington is likely to prevail. The judge said in court that she didn't see "any way" the government could win the case on the merits.   She reiterated that the project lacks congressional approval, which the Trump administration has not sought. It argues that the arch is covered by a 1925 law authorizing a pair of much shorter columns at that same location, which were never built. Both judges have frowned upon that argument.   
   "It hurts your credibility with the court by focusing on that," Brinkema told lawyers Friday, according to Reuters.   Brinkema also called it a "rushed job," and seemed to find the government's analysis of the structure's environmental and economic impact inadequate, particularly concerning the impact of construction cranes — which the government has said would be taller than the arch itself — on airspace.   The Federal Aviation Administration has said the arch would not pose a hazard to aircraft as long as it is lit a certain way, including with a controversial eternal flame on top. But aviation safety experts are concerned that the structure would add an additional layer of risk to an already notoriously complicated airspace. They say that's especially true if it has any military capabilities, which were not included in the FAA's analysis.

schema.headline: A second judge blocks Trump's arch, saying it's unlikely to succeed in court

title: Trump initially accepted the midterm results, but most GOP voters doubt they were fair
description: A firefighter walks past voting booths a
body:
A firefighter walks past voting booths at a firehouse serving as a polling location in Detroit on Nov. 3.
                
                    Spencer Platt/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Spencer Platt/Getty Images
    

   
   President Trump may have initially accepted the results of his party's midterm losses, but data released Friday shows there is still broad distrust in the elections process among Republicans.   Less than half of Republican voters nationwide considered the midterm elections "free and fair," according to new polling by the University of California San Diego. Just 52% of Republicans said they trusted votes were counted accurately.   
   In comparison, after the 2024 election that Trump won, more than 80% of Republicans said they had confidence in the vote-counting process.   While trust in elections often dips for voters of the losing party, the GOP has seen bigger swings in confidence in recent years, as Trump has falsely claimed that U.S. elections are corrupt.   "There are still a lot of people who remain unconvinced that they can trust elections," said Thad Kousser, a co-director of UC San Diego's Center for Transparent and Trusted Elections. "And they're predominantly located in one [political] party."   Overall, a wide majority — 66% — of Americans said they think the midterms were fair. That represents an improvement from before the election, when less than half of U.S. adults said they expected free and fair contests.   But that post-election increase in trust was buoyed by Democrats and independents — many of whom worried before Election Day about potential federal interference at the polls that didn't come to pass.   "It would be a mistake to [look at the 66%] and think, 'Oh, everyone has a pretty good view of the election,'" said Lauren Prather, also a co-director of UC San Diego's election center. "It really buries the lede a little bit about the partisan gap."   
   The widespread doubt among Republicans may be a reality check for those wondering whether Trump's brand of election denial has run its course in American politics.   On the one hand, there will be fewer politicians who deny or question election results in office next year. And the vast majority of election-denying candidates running for positions involved in overseeing statewide elections lost their races this year, according to tracking by the advocacy group States United Action.   Election experts have also celebrated as Trump and high-profile losing candidates on the ballot this year conceded their losses.   "Sure, I'll accept [the results]," Trump told Fox News' Bret Baier on election night, as it became clear Democrats would retake the House and Senate. "Why wouldn't I?"   But just a few days later, he began conspiracy theorizing about those same results.   "Does anybody really believe that this 'Election' was honest," Trump posted online.   The new polling from UC San Diego shows that among Republicans, there still may be a receptive audience to such claims. When asked if politicians are discussing voter fraud too much, too little or about the right amount, just 15% of Republicans answered "too much."   "There is both demand among the Republican base for continued focus on this issue, and as we saw even after the election, politicians are continuing to supply it," Kousser said. "As long as those two dynamics are there, there's still going to be a market for these concerns."   
   To be clear, in most elections — domestically and internationally — supporters of the losing party usually see a dip in trust.   "It's sort of like asking people after an overtime basketball game, do you trust the referees?" Kousser said.   But in an ideal world, he said that oscillation would be more like 10 percentage points in either direction. Not the 30-point swing seen among Republicans between 2024 and 2026.   The numbers do still represent an improvement from 2020, however. At that time, leading up to the Jan. 6 riot at the U.S. Capitol in 2021, just 22% of Republicans said they had confidence in the nationwide vote count, according to similar polling done by MIT's Election Data and Science Lab.

schema.headline: Trump initially accepted the midterm results, but most GOP voters doubt they were fair

title: Trump touts meeting with Xi and Putin but offers few results
description: President Trump speaks as Secretary of S
body:
President Trump speaks as Secretary of State Marco Rubio listens during a news briefing at the White House on Friday. Trump is addressing the media after returning from a visit to China where he held trilateral talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
                
                    Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images
    

   
   President Trump took to the White House briefing room Friday telling reporters his trip to Asia this week – where he met with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin – was a resounding success, despite offering few tangible results.   "The United States entered this trip from a position of unmatched economic and diplomatic strength," Trump said, standing at the podium with VIce President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio behind him.   But the trip resulted more in agreements to continue discussions rather than any concrete changes. The meeting with Putin and Xi, though historic as it was the first time they met, only resulted in an agreement to continue discussing reducing nuclear risks.   
   In Manila, where Trump met with allies before he traveled to China, Trump signed a trade agreement with Thailand. But there are still details to the deal being finalized and the document signed simply marked a "substantial conclusion" in negotiations.   
   At the White House, Trump gave a wide-ranging opening statement to the press that veered from recounting his trip and who he met with, to asides about Iran, the U.S. Federal Reserve, his quest for a Nobel Peace Prize and domestic manufacturing. It was the first time he took questions from the press since being in China.   One significant change Trump announced in the middle of his press remarks was that he and XI have agreed to establish "joint guardrails" on artificial intelligence – a new move from Trump, who has been adamant that regulation over the technology would inhibit US innovation and help China lead in the global AI race. No further details about what the guardrails would look like, when they would be negotiated and released and how they would be applied between the two nations has been announced.   Trump, who said Xi also likes his term "super intelligence" rather than artificial, said, "Problem is, it may be too super. So, President Xi and I agree that we're going to do some joint guardrails, the two of us."   
   The announcement of future guardrails comes as Trump is facing headwinds from growing tech outages in the U.S. that ultimately led to Trump replacing the White House's cyber director.   In the briefing, Trump added that he would continue to push for the construction of data centers in the U.S. This comes after midterm election voters from both parties showed their opposition to future unfettered growth.   
   "Make them pay your community, but take advantage. Don't shut them off," Trump said of the massive complexes that have drawn criticism from communities due to environmental and noise pollution.   He also announced penalizations against companies that try to build data centers outside the U.S.   "If it's not this country, there's somebody else outside. And we're not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country. We're not going to allow that to happen," Trump said.   Trump's trip to China came as Trump's own cabinet on what approach to take toward China. Trump's Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been in favor of selling China U.S. chips, a stance that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang shared. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has expressed a more hawkish view toward China, and Trump has acknowledged both perspectives.   The divide has become more prominent as Lutnick and Trump face backlash for their relationship to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned from his position after admitting to an affair with a woman who may be a Chinese spy.   On Friday, Trump said he only wants "older chips" to be sold to China, rather than the most cutting-edge technology the U.S. has, and he said he'd be OK with no chips going to China at all, though he pointed out the downside to that.   "You have to understand, China makes chips too," Trump said. "And if we're not going to sell them, they'll make them themselves."

schema.headline: Trump touts meeting with Xi and Putin but offers few results

title: Dems aim to block Iran war funding. And, Army delays lead azide detonation in Iowa

Government Funding Pressure On Iran War, National Security & Tech, Iowa Detonation

body:
Government Funding Pressure On Iran War, National Security & Tech, Iowa Detonation
    
            
                
                Transcript

                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    



      Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.   Today's top stories   Democrats who won this month's election are looking to use their influence to block funding for the war in Iran before officially taking charge of Congress. President Trump launched attacks last winter without congressional approval, breaking from the tradition of seeking bipartisan support for wars.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Reporters set up for a press conference outside of the U.S. Capitol Building on Nov. 19, 2026, in Washington, D.C.
                
                    Finn Gomez/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Finn Gomez/Getty Images
    

   
   🎧 Congress must pass a funding measure to avoid a shutdown by Dec. 11. NPR's Claudia Grisales tells Up First that Democrats hold leverage, since their votes are essential for the Republican-controlled Senate to meet the 60-vote threshold. Senate Democrats argue they should use their authority to end what they call an illegal war. Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine aims to include a provision to end war funding in the stopgap bill. Republicans counter that cutting war funding jeopardizes service members in the region. N.C. Republican Sen. Thom Tillis tells Grisales his party may need to explore alternatives if Democrats push for a shutdown. That could include using reconciliation to pass legislation without Democratic votes.   Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping met for the third time this year, underscoring a dilemma for Americans who see China as a business opportunity and a national security risk. Nvidia's former CEO, Jensen Huang, convinced Trump to approve several chip sales before his departure. The House Foreign Affairs Committee yesterday, in a highly unusual step, released a list of requests this year from Nvidia and AMD to sell chips directly to Chinese companies.   
   🎧 The Trump administration approved the sale of nearly 900,000 advanced chips to Chinese companies as of May 2026. Some of those approvals included well-known firms such as Alibaba and Tencent, which the Pentagon lists as having ties to China's military, NPR's Greg Myre says. During his second term, Trump shifted his stance on China, partly influenced by his relationship with Jinping. The two may meet again next month in Miami.   The U.S. Army has rescheduled the detonation of around 9,500 pounds of unstable lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown to Monday, Nov. 23. This decision comes after Iowa lawmakers and two environmental groups pushed for a delay. The plant, which manufactures various types of ammunition, has stored lead azide in a water-ethanol solution in underground tanks for 20 years. Recent inspections found that the tanks were too dry, leading to crystallization and instability. To prevent an accidental explosion, the Army wants to detonate the lead azide under controlled conditions.   🎧 Many Iowans were unaware of the situation until earlier this week, prompting the delay, says Eliza Billingham of NPR network station Iowa Public Radio. Acting Army Secretary Adam R. Telle said on social media that he directed Army Materiel Command to postpone the blasts until the "latest possible moment" before a forecasted drop in temperatures. Army spokesperson Justine Barati previously said that cold weather could make the situation more dangerous. Last month, the Army hosted an informational open house for Middletown residents and shared maps predicting the movement of lead dust. Those maps will need to be revised based on the new forecast, Billingham says. If the detonation proceeds, the Army, EPA and the University of Iowa will monitor air quality.   
   Picture show   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Environmentalist Jassim al-Asadi stands on a boat and looks out over the marshes where he grew up in southern Iraq. Despite having been kidnapped, tortured and accused by an Iran-backed militia of being an Israeli agent, Asadi is back in the marshes.
                
                    Claire Harbage/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Claire Harbage/NPR
    

   
   Iraqi environmentalist Jassim al-Asadi has dedicated his life to protecting Iraq's ancient marshlands. He even helped reflood areas that Saddam Hussein drained and set fire to decades ago to flush out resistance fighters. In February 2023, an Iran-backed militia kidnapped and tortured Asadi for two weeks on false charges that he was an Israeli spy who had ignited anti-government protests. He endured the trauma by reciting poetry until his Bani Asad tribe mobilized armed tribal fighters to secure his release. Once freed, he refused European asylum so he could continue his work. Today, despite drought and other hardships on the land, Asadi continues to monitor recovering water levels as wildlife slowly starts to return to the marshes.   Weekend picks   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Grand Theft Auto VI protagonists, Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, against the backdrop of the Miami-inspired Vice City.
                
                    Rockstar Games
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Rockstar Games
    

   
   Check out what NPR is watching, reading and listening to this weekend:   🍿 Movies: Being Heumann chronicles Judy Heumann, the "mother of the disability rights movement," and her coalition as they embark on a historic 1970s sit-in to advocate for disability rights legislation.   📺 TV: In the new British comedy-fantasy Small Prophets, a man summons magical spirits in an attempt to locate his long-missing girlfriend.   📚 Books: Longtime host of Reading Rainbow LeVar Burton shares his journey in his new memoir, Take My Word for It. He reflects on his life, both in and out of his iconic roles, and the unexpected twists he's encountered.   🎵 Music: On Graceland Way, singer-songwriter and harpist Mikaela Davis blends psychedelic and alternative country, showcasing her boundary-pushing harp play.   🎮 Gaming: After years of waiting, fans can now revel in the Bonnie-and-Clyde love story in Grand Theft Auto VI. The game is poised to steal the crown as the biggest entertainment launch ever with up to $5 billion in projected first-week sales, according to estimates.   ❓ Quiz: What a week! A new James Bond was named, SpaceX made history and the Alaska Senate race was called. Think you were paying attention? Let's find out.   
   3 things to know before you go   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Pilgrims pray in front of the Kaaba, Islam's holiest shrine, at the Grand Mosque in Mecca, Saudi Arabia. Muslims will outnumber Christians by 2070, according to a new report.
                
                    STR/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        STR/AP
    

   
   A new Pew Research Center report shows that by 2035, Muslims will become the largest religious group globally, surpassing Christians.The Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden announced that Fiona, the famous 9-year-old hippo, has died after failing to pass a hat she ingested more than a week ago. (via WVXU)Mayor Zohran Mamdani signed a bill yesterday banning New York City's 160-year-old horse-drawn carriage industry. Animal rights activists have fought for decades to end the practice.
